title: AI credit scoring: the tools, the rules and what to build first
description: Approve more good loans with an AI credit model you can explain: the tools, US and EU rules, three builds and our pick.
summary: AI credit scoring predicts whether an applicant will repay[^5], then has to say why in plain words when it says no[^1][^43]. The model is the easy part. The decline reasons[^1][^41], the bias checks[^39][^40] and the paperwork your examiner will ask for[^7][^8] are what make or break it.
verdict: The payoff is approving more good loans without adding losses; judge it at your own cutoff on your own loans, not vendor claims[^18][^29].
Start with a scorecard you can explain line by line[^17][^16]; it gives the specific decline reasons US law requires straight from the model[^1][^43].
Move to a more complex model only when your own benchmark shows it predicts better and your validators can check it[^5][^7][^41].
Use AI to read loan documents, not to decide: in published studies, language models predicted defaults worse than standard models[^6][^13].
The main software is free; the real cost is your team's time on data, validation and decline reasons[^50][^52][^7][^41].

pickElse: No data science team: look at a platform such as Zest AI, Provenir, Taktile or Scienaptic. None publish prices; expect a contract[^18][^19][^20][^21].

Many thin-file applicants, with little credit history: their scores are less accurate[^40]. Add bank-account cash-flow data from Plaid Check, Prism Data or Nova Credit before you change the model[^27][^28][^30].
Most of the work is reading documents: spend on extraction first (recipe 3 below). In our own benchmark, AI read each long report for under $0.30[^42].

ownData.title: The open-source credit stack, checked 26 November 2026
ownData.intro: For your modeler: release date, licence and monthly downloads for every open-source credit library a lender would use[^45][^58]. Downloads show what teams actually run; release dates show what is still maintained.
ownData.note: Source: PyPI release history and pypistats, pulled 26 November 2026. Stale means no release in over two years. Download counts include CI and build-tool installs[^44], so read them as relative popularity, not user counts.

example.input: An application with income, debts and time at address, plus a credit bureau report pulled with consent.
example.output: A score and an approve or decline. For a decline, the top reasons in plain words, such as "debt is high compared with income", ready for the decline letter (adverse action notice).

recipes.name: 1. Small lender: explainable scorecard
recipes.when: Credit unions and community banks with a small analytics team, or an outside builder. The software is free[^50][^52], and the points table shows each decline reason directly[^17].
flow: Application + credit bureau report
Group each input into ranges and give each range points (optbinning)
Add up the points into a score
Credit officer sets the cutoff and policy rules
Decision with the top decline reasons
A named person sends the decline letter
Quarterly check for accuracy drift and bias (fairlearn)
recipes.cost: Free open-source software[^50][^52]; building it on your past loans is quoted per job, with no price published here. After that, the cost is your team's time for regular reviews.

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size lender: stronger model with plain-English reasons
recipes.when: Fintechs and regional lenders with a team that can validate the model before first use[^7].
flow: Application + bureau + bank-account data
Combine into one table of inputs
Stronger model that weighs many inputs at once (LightGBM)
Find which inputs drove each score (SHAP)
Turn drivers into plain-English reasons; compliance signs them off
Credit officer sets cutoffs in the decision engine
A named person sends the decline letter
Monthly check against a simpler model that shows each input's effect (EBM)
recipes.cost: Open-source models[^71][^47]. Cash-flow data and most decision platforms are quoted per contract[^26][^30][^19][^20]; of the platforms we checked, only Experian shows a public price[^23].

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy files: AI reads, a normal model scores
recipes.when: Small business, mortgage and other files with many PDFs per application.
flow: Bank statements, pay stubs, tax returns
AI pulls out the key fields
People check the shaky ones: an underwriter reviews each field the AI flags
Scorecard or stronger model scores
Decision with reasons
A named person sends the decline letter
recipes.cost: In our own benchmark, AI read fund reports of up to 57 pages for about $0.006 to $0.27 each, depending on the models[^42]. That was measured on fund reports, so benchmark it on your own loan files; see the AI document processing guide[^42].

tables.title: What published studies found
tables.intro: Other teams' results on public data. AUC measures how well a model ranks repayers above defaulters: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Your loan book can differ, which is why you benchmark.

rows.name: arXiv 2510.25701
cells: On LendingClub loans, LightGBM scored an AUC of 0.73; the best language model used with no extra training scored 0.67[^6].

rows.name: FinNLP 2025
cells: XGBoost beat generative language models at forecasting credit ratings[^13].

rows.name: arXiv 2401.16458
cells: A risk score from BERT, an older language model, built from loan descriptions, added to XGBoost, raised AUC slightly, from 0.658 to 0.664[^14].

rows.name: arXiv 2605.18147
cells: TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2 had the best average across 14 default datasets, with the biggest gains on small or unbalanced sets[^15].

rows.name: MDPI review, 2026
cells: XGBoost leads on accuracy, logistic regression holds up on small data, and SHAP is the standard explainer[^5].

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: A lender that declines an applicant must give the specific main reasons within 30 days, and they must match the factors the model actually scored[^1]. Every model needs a clean path from its output to plain-English reasons. Name one person who sends each decline letter on time.

rules.name: CFPB circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03
rules.what: They said complex algorithms are no excuse for vague reasons[^43]. The guidance is gone; the rule it explained is not[^2][^1]. Don't read the withdrawal as a pass.

rules.name: Fed SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13, model risk guidance
rules.what: This mostly doesn't apply below $30 billion in assets; smaller banks are generally excluded[^3][^7]. The OCC adopted it and dropped its 1997 credit-scoring exam guide[^8]. Where it applies, validate models before first use and document them; generative and agentic AI are out of scope[^7].

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Scoring people's creditworthiness is high-risk; fraud detection is exempt[^4]. Lenders using it must assign trained human oversight and keep its logs[^11], and do a fundamental rights impact assessment[^12]. Plan now if you lend in the EU.

howToTest: Record today's numbers first: approval rate, loss rate, time to decision and share of files reviewed by hand.
Take two to three years of your booked loans with known outcomes, and hold out the most recent months as the test.
Fit three models on the same data, inputs and split: a scorecard, an EBM and LightGBM. An EBM (Explainable Boosting Machine) shows each input's effect; LightGBM is stronger but harder to explain.

For a small loan book, try TabPFN too, a ready-trained AI model for tables[^15]. It did best on small, unbalanced default data in one 2026 study[^15], but its newest weights need a commercial licence for production[^49].
Compare AUC and KS on the held-out months. Both measure how well a model separates repayers from defaulters; AUC runs from 0.5, a coin flip, to 1.0, perfect.
Turn each model's output into decline reasons, and check they stay the same when you refit on a new sample.
Price the lift in dollars at your cutoff: the extra approvals you gain and the losses you avoid. That tells you what a better model is worth.
Run a bias check across the groups fair-lending exams look at, using fairlearn or your own approval-gap analysis.
Pick the simplest model within a point or two of the best. Extra accuracy that you cannot explain costs more than it earns.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a platform when you have no modelling team, need a decision engine anyway, and are happy to use the vendor's models and data partners. Expect a quote, not a price list[^18][^19][^20].
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your own loan history is your edge. The main scorecard and boosting libraries are free under MIT or Apache licences[^50][^45][^71], and examiners judge any model by its validation and documentation[^7]. The work is data, validation and reason codes[^41].

watchOuts: A credit report's "key factors" list does not count as your decline reasons[^1]. Your model must produce its own[^1][^43].

SHAP shows which inputs drove a score, but it does not write Regulation B reasons, and some versions miss the true ones[^41][^5]. Group related inputs into a reason-code map that compliance signs off[^41].
Models trained on past lending data can carry past bias forward[^39][^40]. Check approval gaps before launch and every quarter after, with a tool such as fairlearn[^52].
TabPFN's newest weights are non-commercial[^49]. Check the licence before production use.
Vendor lift numbers such as more approvals are measured on the vendor's chosen data[^18][^28][^29]. Ask for a benchmark on your own loans.
